lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: CHAPTER XII. Alice’s Evidence

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Here!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice, quite forgetting in the flurry of the moment how large she had grown in the last few minutes, and she jumped up in such a hurry that she tipped over the jury-box with the edge of her skirt, upsetting all the jurymen on to the heads of the crowd below, and there they lay sprawling about, reminding her very much of a globe of goldfish she had accidentally upset the week before.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh, I beg your pardon!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she exclaimed in a tone of great dismay, and began picking them up again as quickly as she could, for the accident of the goldfish kept running in her head, and she had a vague sort of idea that they must be collected at once and put back into the jury-box, or they would die.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “The trial cannot proceed,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King in a very grave voice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “until all the jurymen are back in their proper places—all,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he repeated with great emphasis, looking hard at Alice as he said so. Alice looked at the jury-box, and saw that, in her haste, she had put the Lizard in head downwards, and the poor little thing was waving its tail about in a melancholy way, being quite unable to move. She soon got it out again, and put it right;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “not that it signifies much,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said to herself;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I should think it would be quite as much use in the trial one way up as the other.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: As soon as the jury had a little recovered from the shock of being upset, and their slates and pencils had been found and handed back to them, they set to work very diligently to write out a history of the accident, all except the Lizard, who seemed too much overcome to do anything but sit with its mouth open, gazing up into the roof of the court.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “What do you know about this business?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King said to Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Nothing,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Nothing whatever?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: persisted the King.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Nothing whatever,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “That’s very important,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King said, turning to the jury. They were just beginning to write this down on their slates, when the White Rabbit interrupted:

lines.speaker: White Rabbit
lines.text: “Unimportant, your Majesty means, of course,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said in a very respectful tone, but frowning and making faces at him as he spoke.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Unimportant, of course, I meant,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King hastily said, and went on to himself in an undertone,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “important—unimportant—unimportant—important—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: as if he were trying which word sounded best. Some of the jury wrote it down “important,” and some

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “unimportant.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice could see this, as she was near enough to look over their slates;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “but it doesn’t matter a bit,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she thought to herself. At this moment the King, who had been for some time busily writing in his note-book, cackled out “Silence!” and read out from his book,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Rule Forty-two. All persons more than a mile high to leave the court.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Everybody looked at Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’m not a mile high,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “You are,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Nearly two miles high,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: added the Queen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Well, I shan’t go, at any rate,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “besides, that’s not a regular rule: you invented it just now.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It’s the oldest rule in the book,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Then it ought to be Number One,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice. The King turned pale, and shut his note-book hastily.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Consider your verdict,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said to the jury, in a low, trembling voice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “There’s more evidence to come yet, please your Majesty,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the White Rabbit, jumping up in a great hurry;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “this paper has just been picked up.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “What’s in it?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Queen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I haven’t opened it yet,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the White Rabbit,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “but it seems to be a letter, written by the prisoner to—to somebody.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It must have been that,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “unless it was written to nobody, which isn’t usual, you know.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Who is it directed to?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said one of the jurymen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It isn’t directed at all,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the White Rabbit;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “in fact, there’s nothing written on the outside.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He unfolded the paper as he spoke, and added

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It isn’t a letter, after all: it’s a set of verses.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Are they in the prisoner’s handwriting?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: asked another of the jurymen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “No, they’re not,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the White Rabbit,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and that’s the queerest thing about it.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: (The jury all looked puzzled.)

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “He must have imitated somebody else’s hand,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King. (The jury all brightened up again.)

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Please your Majesty,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Knave,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I didn’t write it, and they can’t prove I did: there’s no name signed at the end.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If you didn’t sign it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “that only makes the matter worse. You must have meant some mischief, or else you’d have signed your name like an honest man.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: There was a general clapping of hands at this: it was the first really clever thing the King had said that day.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “That proves his guilt,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Queen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It proves nothing of the sort!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Why, you don’t even know what they’re about!”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Read them,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King. The White Rabbit put on his spectacles.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Where shall I begin, please your Majesty?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he asked.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Begin at the beginning,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King said gravely,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: These were the verses the White Rabbit read:—

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “They told me you had been to her, And mentioned me to him: She gave me a good character, But said I could not swim. He sent them word I had not gone (We know it to be true): If she should push the matter on, What would become of you? I gave her one, they gave him two, You gave us three or more; They all returned from him to you, Though they were mine before. If I or she should chance to be Involved in this affair, He trusts to you to set them free, Exactly as we were. My notion was that you had been (Before she had this fit) An obstacle that came between Him, and ourselves, and it. Don’t let him know she liked them best, For this must ever be A secret, kept from all the rest, Between yourself and me.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “That’s the most important piece of evidence we’ve heard yet,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King, rubbing his hands;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “so now let the jury—”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If any one of them can explain it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, (she had grown so large in the last few minutes that she wasn’t a bit afraid of interrupting him),

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’ll give him sixpence. I don’t believe there’s an atom of meaning in it.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The jury all wrote down on their slates,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “She doesn’t believe there’s an atom of meaning in it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: but none of them attempted to explain the paper.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If there’s no meaning in it,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “that saves a world of trouble, you know, as we needn’t try to find any. And yet I don’t know,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he went on, spreading out the verses on his knee, and looking at them with one eye;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I seem to see some meaning in them, after all. “—said I could not swim—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: you can’t swim, can you?” he added, turning to the Knave. The Knave shook his head sadly.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Do I look like it?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said. (Which he certainly did not, being made entirely of cardboard.)

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “All right, so far,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King, and he went on muttering over the verses to himself:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “‘We know it to be true—’ that’s the jury, of course—‘I gave her one, they gave him two—’ why, that must be what he did with the tarts, you know—”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “But, it goes on ‘they all returned from him to you,’”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Why, there they are!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King triumphantly, pointing to the tarts on the table.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Nothing can be clearer than that. Then again—‘before she had this fit—’ you never had fits, my dear, I think?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: he said to the Queen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Never!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Queen furiously, throwing an inkstand at the Lizard as she spoke. (The unfortunate little Bill had left off writing on his slate with one finger, as he found it made no mark; but he now hastily began again, using the ink, that was trickling down his face, as long as it lasted.)

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Then the words don’t fit you,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the King, looking round the court with a smile. There was a dead silence.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It’s a pun!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King added in an offended tone, and everybody laughed,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Let the jury consider their verdict.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the King said, for about the twentieth time that day.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “No, no!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Queen.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Sentence first—verdict afterwards.”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Stuff and nonsense!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice loudly.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “The idea of having the sentence first!”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Hold your tongue!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said the Queen, turning purple.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I won’t!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Off with her head!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: the Queen shouted at the top of her voice. Nobody moved.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Who cares for you?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time).

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “You’re nothing but a pack of cards!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: At this the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her: she gave a little scream, half of fright and half of anger, and tried to beat them off, and found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister, who was gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Wake up, Alice dear!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said her sister;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Why, what a long sleep you’ve had!”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, and she told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all these strange Adventures of hers that you have just been reading about; and when she had finished, her sister kissed her, and said,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “It was a curious dream, dear, certainly: but now run in to your tea; it’s getting late.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So Alice got up and ran off, thinking while she ran, as well she might, what a wonderful dream it had been. But her sister sat still just as she left her, leaning her head on her hand, watching the setting sun, and thinking of little Alice and all her wonderful Adventures, till she too began dreaming after a fashion, and this was her dream:— First, she dreamed of little Alice herself, and once again the tiny hands were clasped upon her knee, and the bright eager eyes were looking up into hers—she could hear the very tones of her voice, and see that queer little toss of her head to keep back the wandering hair that would always get into her eyes—and still as she listened, or seemed to listen, the whole place around her became alive with the strange creatures of her little sister’s dream. The long grass rustled at her feet as the White Rabbit hurried by—the frightened Mouse splashed his way through the neighbouring pool—she could hear the rattle of the teacups as the March Hare and his friends shared their never-ending meal, and the shrill voice of the Queen ordering off her unfortunate guests to execution—once more the pig-baby was sneezing on the Duchess’s knee, while plates and dishes crashed around it—once more the shriek of the Gryphon, the squeaking of the Lizard’s slate-pencil, and the choking of the suppressed guinea-pigs, filled the air, mixed up with the distant sobs of the miserable Mock Turtle. So she sat on, with closed eyes, and half believed herself in Wonderland, though she knew she had but to open them again, and all would change to dull reality—the grass would be only rustling in the wind, and the pool rippling to the waving of the reeds—the rattling teacups would change to tinkling sheep-bells, and the Queen’s shrill cries to the voice of the shepherd boy—and the sneeze of the baby, the shriek of the Gryphon, and all the other queer noises, would change (she knew) to the confused clamour of the busy farm-yard—while the lowing of the cattle in the distance would take the place of the Mock Turtle’s heavy sobs. Lastly, she pictured to herself how this same little sister of hers would, in the after-time, be herself a grown woman; and how she would keep, through all her riper years, the simple and loving heart of her childhood: and how she would gather about her other little children, and make their eyes bright and eager with many a strange tale, perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland of long ago: and how she would feel with all their simple sorrows, and find a pleasure in all their simple joys, remembering her own child-life, and the happy summer days. THE END
